lead: An inner product takes two vectors and returns a single number. From that one number you get everything geometric: the length of a vector, the distance between two vectors, and the angle between them. This is how linear algebra talks about shape, not just algebra. It is used wherever a computer must compare signals, images or text: recommender systems score how similar two users are, and a telecom engineer measures how far a received symbol sits from the ideal one. Some syllabi call the inner product the scalar product or the dot product.
prereq: You need: vectors, linear combinations and basis from Unit 2, Vector Spaces.

sections.h3: The inner product as a rule

blocks.text: An inner product is a rule that takes two vectors u and v from a vector space and returns one number, written ⟨u, v⟩. The brackets ⟨ ⟩ are read as "inner product of". The rule is not arbitrary; it must obey three axioms over the reals.

items: Positive definite: ⟨u, u⟩ ≥ 0, and ⟨u, u⟩ = 0 only when u = 0.
Linear in the first slot: ⟨αu + βw, v⟩ = α⟨u, v⟩ + β⟨w, v⟩ for real numbers α and β.

blocks.text: Over the complex numbers the second axiom changes to ⟨u, v⟩ = conjugate of ⟨v, u⟩. Write the conjugate of a complex number z as z̄. Then ⟨u, αv⟩ = ᾱ⟨u, v⟩: the rule is linear in the first slot and conjugate-linear in the second. The quantity ⟨u, u⟩ is always a non-negative real number, even in a complex space.

blocks.where: u = (u₁, …, uₙ) and v = (v₁, …, vₙ) are vectors in ℝⁿ and uᵢ, vᵢ are real numbers. This is the standard dot product on ℝⁿ.
w₁, …, wₙ are fixed positive weights. Each coordinate is counted more or less heavily. In ℝ² with w = (1, 4), u = (1, 1) and v = (1, −1) give ⟨u, v⟩ = 1·1·1 + 4·1·(−1) = 1 − 4 = −3.
f and g are polynomials in the variable x, and the integral runs from x = 0 to x = 1. For f(x) = 1 and g(x) = x, ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀¹ x dx = 1/2. Vectors are now functions, not lists of numbers.

blocks.text: The inner product of a vector with itself gives its squared length. The norm is the square root of that.

blocks.where: ‖u‖ is the norm (length) of u; d(u, v) is the distance between u and v; u − v is the vector difference.

blocks.text: The norm behaves as length should. ‖u‖ ≥ 0, with equality only for u = 0. Scaling a vector scales its length by the absolute value of the scalar: ‖cu‖ = |c|‖u‖. For example, ‖(3, 4)‖ = √(9 + 16) = 5 in ℝ², and ‖2·(3, 4)‖ = 10. Every non-zero vector has a unit vector u/‖u‖ of length 1 pointing the same way.

The weights change the lengths. With w = (1, 4) in ℝ², ‖(1, 1)‖ = √(1·1 + 4·1) = √5 ≈ 2.236, not √2. The same list of numbers carries different lengths under different inner products, so always state which rule you use.
In the polynomial space with ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀¹ f g dx, ⟨x, x⟩ = ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3, so ‖x‖ = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577. A shorter distance means two functions are close everywhere on [0, 1] in the average sense.
Two more properties, the triangle inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, follow from the axioms and decide when a rule is a genuine norm; they are proved in 5.2.
In ℝ² and ℝ³ the usual geometric formula for the dot product rearranges into a definition of angle that works in any inner product space.

blocks.where: θ is the angle between the non-zero vectors u and v, measured in radians or degrees; the denominator is the product of the two norms.

blocks.text: In ℝ², u = (3, 4) and v = (1, 0) give ⟨u, v⟩ = 3, ‖u‖ = 5, ‖v‖ = 1, so cos θ = 3/5 and θ ≈ 53.13°. The formula agrees with the picture drawn on paper.

A zero inner product means cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°: the vectors are perpendicular, or orthogonal. A negative inner product means an obtuse angle. Tests will ask you to compute the angle rather than to draw it, and the whole calculation rests on the three numbers ⟨u, v⟩, ‖u‖, ‖v‖.
Orthogonal and orthonormal sets, and their use as coordinates, are built on this single formula; see 5.3.

figure.caption: Two vectors give one inner product; the inner product of a vector with itself gives its length; the inner product divided by both lengths gives the cosine of the angle.

spec.title: From inner product to angle
spec.aria: A four-box flow showing that a pair of vectors gives an inner product, the inner product gives a norm, and both give the cosine of the angle.

examples.question: In ℝ³, using the standard dot product, take u = (1, 2, 2) and v = (3, 0, 4). Find ⟨u, v⟩, ‖u‖, ‖v‖, the angle θ between u and v, and the distance d(u, v).
examples.answer: ⟨u, v⟩ = 11; ‖u‖ = 3 and ‖v‖ = 5; the angle θ ≈ 42.83°; the distance d(u, v) = √12 ≈ 3.4641.
examples.check:
import math
u = (1, 2, 2)
v = (3, 0, 4)
ip = sum(a*b for a, b in zip(u, v))
nu = math.sqrt(sum(a*a for a in u))
nv = math.sqrt(sum(b*b for b in v))
cos_t = ip / (nu * nv)
theta = math.degrees(math.acos(cos_t))
d = math.sqrt(sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(u, v)))
print(ip)
print(nu)
print(nv)
print(round(cos_t, 4))
print(round(theta, 2))
print(round(d, 4))

traps: The inner product of a vector with itself is not its length. ⟨(3, 4), (3, 4)⟩ = 25, while the length is √25 = 5. Always take the square root for the norm.
Over ℂ the inner product is conjugate-linear in the second slot, so ⟨u, v⟩ is the conjugate of ⟨v, u⟩. Swapping the order without conjugating gives a wrong sign on the imaginary part.

A weighted inner product needs every weight strictly positive. With w = (1, −1) you get ⟨(1, 1), (1, 1)⟩ = 0 for a non-zero vector, so the rule fails positive definiteness and is not an inner product.
⟨u, v⟩ = 0 does not mean u or v is the zero vector. It means the two vectors are perpendicular. Examiners often give a zero inner product and ask what follows — the answer is orthogonality.
A negative inner product is not an error. It gives cos θ < 0, so θ is greater than 90°; report the angle in degrees or radians as asked.

quiz.q: State the three axioms of an inner product on a real vector space.
quiz.a: (1) ⟨u, u⟩ ≥ 0, with equality only for u = 0. (2) ⟨u, v⟩ = ⟨v, u⟩. (3) ⟨αu + βw, v⟩ = α⟨u, v⟩ + β⟨w, v⟩ for real α, β.

quiz.q: Why is ⟨u, v⟩ = w₁u₁v₁ + w₂u₂v₂ with w₁ = 1, w₂ = −1 not an inner product on ℝ²?
quiz.a: Positivity fails. Take u = (1, 1): ⟨u, u⟩ = 1·1·1 + (−1)·1·1 = 0, but u ≠ 0. The axiom needs equality only for the zero vector, so all weights must be strictly positive.

quiz.q: In ℝ³ find the angle between u = (1, 0, 1) and v = (1, 2, 2).
On polynomials with ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀¹ f(x)g(x) dx, take f(x) = 1 + x and g(x) = x. Find ⟨f, g⟩, ‖f‖ and ‖g‖.
In ℂ² define ⟨u, v⟩ = u₁v̄₁ + u₂v̄₂. For u = (1, i) and v = (1, 1), compute ⟨u, v⟩ and ⟨v, u⟩ and comment.
quiz.a: ⟨u, v⟩ = 1·1 + i·1 = 1 + i. ⟨v, u⟩ = 1·1 + 1·(conjugate of i) = 1 − i. They are conjugates, not equal, which confirms conjugate symmetry. Also ⟨u, u⟩ = 1·1 + i·(conjugate of i) = 1 + 1 = 2, real and positive, so ‖u‖ = √2.

quiz.q: Show that if ⟨u, v⟩ = 0 for every vector v in the space, then u = 0.
quiz.a: The property holds for every v, so choose v = u. Then ⟨u, u⟩ = 0. By positive definiteness, ⟨u, u⟩ = 0 forces u = 0. This trick — choosing v = u — is the standard way to prove that an inner-product statement forces a vector to vanish.

quiz.q: A student writes ‖u‖ = ⟨u, u⟩. Give a counterexample and explain the correct relation.
quiz.a: Take u = (3, 4). Then ⟨u, u⟩ = 25 but the length is 5. The correct relation is ‖u‖ = √⟨u, u⟩; the inner product gives squared length.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same three axioms, with the integral inner product on functions, lead to Hilbert spaces, the setting for Fourier series and for the quantum state vector. Machine learning uses inner products without ever writing them as coordinates: a kernel function is an inner product in some higher-dimensional space, which is how support vector machines separate curved data. Search for "reproducing kernel Hilbert space", "Hilbert space", "kernel trick" and "inner product in signal detection" if you want to go further.
